Competitive research · Delivery and transportation · Nov 2026

How Uber, DoorDash, Grab and Careem get people from the website to their first trip

A study of marketing sites, web booking flows and mobile first-run across ride-hailing and delivery products, with a close look at how they verify identity without slowing the first order. Prepared for ONGO, an on-demand car wash app in Doha.

UberUber EatsDoorDashDoorDash DasherGrabCareeminDriveFreenow by LyftBlaBlaCartalabatZiplineOpenTableZoox
Summary

Five things the best products agree on

The task is the heroUber's and DoorDash's homepages open with the booking input itself: pickup and drop-off, or a delivery address. Brand storytelling comes second.
Value before identityThe route, the address or the store list comes before any login. Uber's signed-out homepage leads with a route and "See prices" instead of a sign-up button; DoorDash lists stores before sign-up; Grab and Careem let you browse the home screen as a guest.
One identifier, then a codeEvery first run asks for a phone number (or email, Apple, Google) on one screen, then a 4–6 digit code. No passwords at sign-up on mobile.
Verify by risk, not by defaultCustomers prove a phone number. ID and selfie checks appear only when a specific action needs them: the Uber Eats account check, BlaBlaCar trust badges, DoorDash courier onboarding.
Explain every askHeavy checks come with "Why do you need this?" notes, retry tips, a progress bar and an honest wait time, as in the DoorDash Dasher background check.
1 · Marketing websites

Two hero strategies: do the task, or sell the idea

Products people use weekly (rides, food) put a working input in the hero. Products still explaining themselves (drone delivery, robotaxis) lead with a big image and send people to the app.

What the leaders do differently

  • The first field is the product. Uber's pickup field and DoorDash's address field start the real flow; whatever you type carries into the next screen.
  • The page knows where you are. Uber centres the map on your city; OpenTable asks "It looks like you're in Manhattan. Not correct?"
  • The app handoff is a QR code, not a store badge. Uber's signed-in web home ends with "It's easier in the apps": one QR card for riders and one for drivers.
  • Business gets its own front door. Zipline Business and Uber for Business have separate pages with a lead form, not a tab on the consumer page.
2 · Web app flows

Booking on the web: price first, account last

DoorDash lets signed-out visitors set an address and browse every store; Uber's signed-out page starts the route before asking who you are. Sign-in comes when it is needed to finish, and DoorDash opens it over the page so context is kept.

Uber web: request a ride

Pickup + drop-off on the homepage→See prices→Sign in: phone or email→Choose a ride: price range + ETA→Confirm request

DoorDash web: address, browse, then sign up

Delivery address→Adjust pin→Browse stores (signed out)→Sign up modal→6-digit SMS code

4 · Identity and compliance

How they verify identity without slowing the first order

No product in this set asks a customer for an ID at sign-up. Checks are layered: each level is asked for only when an action needs it, and the heaviest checks are reserved for people who will work on the platform.

Level 0 · AnonymousBrowse and priceAsked: nothing
Uber web prices, DoorDash stores, Grab and Careem guest home.
Level 1 · AccountPhone or email + codeAsked: when you book or order
SMS, WhatsApp or a call; Apple and Google as shortcuts.
Level 2 · PaymentCard or walletAsked: at the first checkout
Grab parks "Add a card" on home; Uber shows the card beside "Request".
Level 3 · IdentityID + live selfieAsked: only for a gated action
Uber Eats account check; BlaBlaCar "Verify ID" for a trust badge.
Level 4 · ProviderID, face scan, background checkAsked: before someone can work
DoorDash Dasher: licence, SSN, face scan, safety course.

Customers: verification as a status, not a gate

Uber Eats shows "Not verified" quietly on the account page and only asks when an order needs it. The verify screen offers a choice of method, says who will not see the data, and puts the biometric consent in plain words before the camera opens.

Providers: heavy checks, carefully paced

DoorDash's courier app asks for far more (vehicle, licence, social security number, a face scan) but keeps it moving: a progress bar, one question per screen, answers to the obvious worries, and access to the app while the background check runs.

6 · Best practices

What the field converges on

Website

  • Put the first step of the task in the hero, and carry what people type into the next screen.
  • Detect the city; let people correct it in one tap.
  • Show real prices and times before asking for an account.
  • On desktop, hand off to the app with a QR code; on phones, one store button.
  • Give businesses a separate page with a sales form.

First run

  • One identifier screen: phone first, with Apple, Google or email as shortcuts.
  • A 4–6 digit code with a timer, a resend, and a second channel (call, WhatsApp, backup code).
  • Confirm location with a yes/no, not a form.
  • Land on a usable home screen; park name, email and payment as optional chips.
  • Let guests browse where the product allows it.

Identity and compliance

  • Ask for each level of proof only when an action needs it.
  • Say why, who will see it, and how long it is kept, before the camera opens.
  • Offer more than one method where possible (ID + selfie, or an existing verified account).
  • Give live capture feedback and specific retry tips.
  • Run slow checks in the background and let people into the app with an honest estimate.
  • Reward completion with a visible "Verified" badge.
7 · For ONGO

What this means for ONGO

ONGO's app already does several of these: prices before sign-up, phone and code sign-in with Apple and Google, and a card hold that is charged after the wash. The gaps are on the web and on the washer side.

Customers

  • Website hero: a car-location field (with "Adjust pin") and "See prices", which continues into the app or a sign-up step, as Uber and DoorDash do.
  • Code fallback: add WhatsApp delivery or "Receive a code via call", since many Qatar users live in WhatsApp.
  • No ID for customers: a phone number and a card hold are enough for a car wash; don't add ID checks to the first order.
  • Consents: keep live location separate from marketing, as Freenow does.

Washers (later)

  • Use the Dasher pattern: progress bar, one ask per screen, a face scan with retry tips.
  • Explain the checks: trade licence, CR and Qatar ID, each with a "why we need this" note.
  • Don't block on review: let new washers into the app with a checklist and an honest review time.
  • Tell customers: keep the "licence-verified" promise visible on the site and in booking.
